title: Toronto police officer demoted for refusing to intervene in suicide, lying about being on another call - Winnipeg Free Press
subtitle: Breaking News, Sports, Manitoba, Canada
article: Hey there, time traveller!
This article was published 06/07/2021 (1518 days ago), so information in it may no longer be current.
Warning: Graphic content

More than five years after he refused to intervene in a young man's death by suicide in High Park, then lied about being on another call, a Toronto police officer has been demoted in rank for two years for his "serious" misconduct.

Const. Kyle Upjohn pleaded guilty at a Toronto police disciplinary tribunal to neglect of duty stemming from a high-profile Feb. 2, 2016 incident that began when a desperate citizen tried to get the officer to stop a young man from hanging himself in the park.

Instead, Upjohn - on duty and in a marked cruiser near the entry to the park - refused. He falsely claimed to be on another call, told the concerned citizen, Sasa Vukobrat, to call 911, then drove away.

Vukobrat was left to attempt to save the 19-year-old man's life on his own, including by holding the young man up then cutting him down from a tree while taking instructions from a 911 dispatcher, tribunal documents state.
Upjohn was soon dispatched back to the scene he'd just fled, accompanying the man, later identified as Alexandre Boucher, to the hospital where he was pronounced dead.

"You told the citizen that you were on a call when, in fact, you were not. You drove out of the immediate area only to be detailed to the very call you attempted to avoid," reads a summary of the allegations contained in a penalty decision released by Supt. Riyaz Hussein Tuesday.
"You were neglectful in assisting the citizen who approached you and the person in crisis, who was successful in taking his life," the document states.
According to an agreed statement of facts filed with the tribunal, there was "no evidence" Upjohn could have prevented the young man's death.

Upjohn - who has been suspended with pay since the Feb. 2, 2016, incident - was sentenced to a two-year rank reduction that will result in the loss of approximately $30,000 the first year. According to the Toronto police 2021 salaries, a fourth-class constable makes $73,000 while first class earns $104,000.

In a joint submission last month, Upjohn's lawyer Gary Clewley and Toronto police prosecutor Noah Schachter had argued the rank reduction was the appropriate sentence. Clewley told the tribunal that Upjohn apologizes for his conduct and called it an "aberration," according to Hussein's decision.

The penalty decision ends a five-year saga that saw Ontario's highest court weigh the thorny legal question of whether Upjohn's failure to stop a suicide constituted criminal behaviour - specifically, breach of trust.

In 2016, a few months after Boucher's death, Ontario's police watchdog charged Upjohn with one count each of criminal negligence causing death, failure to provide the necessities of life and breach of trust.

Crown lawyers later withdrew all but the breach of trust charges after the prosecutors were unable to determine the precise time of Boucher's death, meaning there was no way to link Upjohn's failure to act with the cause of death.

After a 2017 preliminary hearing, an Ontario court judge ordered Upjohn to stand trial for breach of trust - a charge laid when an official is accused of breaching the standard of responsibility and conduct demanded by their office.

Upjohn appealed the decision on the grounds that the breach of trust charge did not apply. Clewley, his lawyer, argued there was no evidence Upjohn avoided the call for a corrupt or dishonest ulterior purpose - a component required by the law. Instead, it was negligence that did not rise above professional misconduct, Clewley argued.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Maureen Forestell agreed, quashing the case after finding that although Upjohn's motive may have been to "put his own comfort or needs before the good of the public" this was not enough evidence to prove a breach of trust.

Crown lawyers appealed the decision to Ontario's top court, where a panel of three judges unanimously found there was no evidence to prove Upjohn acted "for a dishonest, partial, corrupt or oppressive purpose."

"However egregious (Upjohn's) conduct may have been, and however seriously such conduct might tarnish the image of his police service and its members, no intent to use the public office for some improper purpose can be inferred from the record," the Court of Appeal ruled.
Upjohn initially faced insubordination and discreditable conduct charges under Ontario's Police Services Act, but they were withdrawn after he pleaded guilty to neglect of duty last month.

At a virtual hearing Tuesday, Hussein said Upjohn's misconduct was "serious," noting the circumstances around his actions "involved neglecting the repeated pleas of a member of the public for assistance, and further misleading a member of the public."
Hussein said: "His actions demonstrated a lack of judgment and were not in keeping with the expectations of a police officer."
The unusual case garnered significant local and national media coverage, causing a hit to the service's reputation that was an aggravating factor in sentencing, Hussein said in his decision.
He noted Upjohn had an otherwise unblemished criminal record, had taken responsibility for his actions by pleading guilty and showed a strong potential for rehabilitation.

"PC Upjohn is taking positive steps based on the information before me. I'm sure he's learned much from these events, but I'm also confident that once this matter is behind him, he will return to being a productive member of the service," Hussein said.

If you are thinking of suicide or know someone who is, there is help. Resources are available online at www.crisisservicescanada.ca or you can connect to the national suicide prevention helpline at 1-833-456-4566, or the Kids Help Phone at 1-800-668-6868.
